newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - gas oil holding up.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - gas oil holding up.

text.p: Gas oil and naphtha markets in the Gulf are the strongest candidates to hold up in the coming week on buoyant Asian demand, Gulf traders said on Thursday.
Kerosene, in contrast, is expected to remain seasonally depressed as temperatures rise while fuel oil's fortunes will remain tied to volatile crude markets, they said.
"IOC's (India Oil Corp) gas oil tender was generally welcomed by the market...it was two cargoes more than expected," a Gulf-based trader said, referring to IOC's May tender.
IOC bought 870,000 tonnes of gas oil (diesel) this week with four of the 21 cargoes going to Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC).

Though the majority of cargoes were priced on a Mediterranean basis, traders said that Gulf gas oil premiums had moved 5-10 cents higher to 44-55 cents on the back of firm Indian demand and tighter March delivery markets in Singapore.
"Indian demand is looking more bullish in the new financial year," a trader said, referring back to budget constraints in the first two months of the year which capped IOC's imports.

Upcoming middle distillate tenders from Sri Lanka for April delivery and from Nepal for May delivery would also support premiums in the short-term despite heavy prices losses in Singapore and Europe on Thursday, traders said.
Gas oil was priced around $25.30 a barrel fob Gulf.

The gas oil-kerosene spread was expected to widen as demand for kerosene faltered, traders said. Kerosene was priced around $24 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, versus $25.20 last week, with premiums assessed at 20-30 cents.
"Kerosene is going through a bad patch...IOC is not looking like it will turn the market around," said one trader.
IOC's tender for superior kerosene closes April 3.

A term tender between KPC and Indonesian state oil firm Pertamina for the supply of a 55,000 tonne cargo of Kuwaiti jet every 40 days was unlikely to take pressure off the spot market in the Gulf, traders said.

Naphtha premiums in the Gulf remained strong at around $15 a tonne, led higher by strong Far East petrochemical demand which prompted Saudi Aramco to consider importing gasoline in April to maximise naphtha exports, traders said.
Gulf naphtha was assessed around $201 a tonne on Thursday.
Fujairah 380-cst bunkers were steady at $98 a tonne.
